nameStory: Korean grass gets its name from its East Asian origins, though it's also called Japanese lawngrass since it's native to the coastal grasslands of southeast Asia, including Japan and Korea. The scientific name Zoysia honors Karl von Zoys, an 18th-century Austrian botanist who studied grasses.
description: Korean grass is a low-growing, dense perennial grass that spreads by creeping underground stems (rhizomes) and above-ground runners (stolons) to form thick, carpet-like mats. This warm-season grass typically stays quite short, rarely growing taller than 2-3 inches when unmowed. Originally from coastal Asia, it was introduced to the United States in 1895 and has become a popular alternative to other lawn grasses, though it's still uncommon in New England's cooler climate.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, thick mats that feel springy and cushion-like underfoot, spreading by both underground rhizomes and surface runners that root at nodes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, stiff blades that feel somewhat rough and wiry to the touch, with a distinctive rolled or folded appearance rather than flat

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The turf feels noticeably denser and more cushioned than typical cool-season grasses, almost like walking on a thick carpet

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Deep green in summer but turns brown or dormant much earlier in fall than cool-season grasses, staying brown through winter

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces small, inconspicuous seed heads on short stalks in late summer, but rarely flowers in New England's climate

habitat: In New England, Korean grass is almost exclusively found in maintained lawns, particularly in warmer, protected areas with good drainage. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, and is most likely to be encountered in southern New England where temperatures are more favorable for this warm-season grass.

seasonality.spring: Begins greening up much later than cool-season grasses, often not until late May or June when soil temperatures warm significantly.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush, deep green color and active spreading through runners and underground stems.
seasonality.fall: Goes dormant and turns brown much earlier than other lawn grasses, typically by mid to late September.
seasonality.winter: Remains completely brown and dormant, looking almost dead compared to the evergreen cool-season grasses common in New England.

funFact: Korean grass was first brought to America in 1895 from Manchuria and became so popular that it's now used on golf courses worldwide, but it grows so slowly that establishing a new Korean grass lawn can take 2-3 years compared to just weeks for other grasses!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dense lawn grasses, but Korean grass's distinctive late spring green-up and early fall dormancy make it stand out - remember "Korean grass sleeps longer" since it stays brown when cool-season grasses are green in spring and fall.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called both Korean grass and Japanese lawngrass, this species is native to a much broader region of coastal Southeast Asia. The confusion in common names reflects the different countries from which it was first collected and introduced to various parts of the world.
compareHints: Korean grass differs from its close relative Manila grass by being more cold-tolerant and having coarser, wider leaf blades. Unlike the fine, soft texture of Manila grass, Korean grass feels notably stiffer and more wiry to the touch, making it the hardier choice for transitional climates like southern New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Manila grass differs from its relative Korean grass (the only other Zoysia species that might survive in New England) by having finer leaves and a more prostrate, mat-forming growth habit.
